**The code was never the problem. On the new 30-pin board the two I²C wires are reversed: the wire on D21 carries the MCX clock, and the wire on D22 carries data.** Swap those two jumpers at the ESP32 end and the gateway comes up.

**How I confirmed it.** Both boards are plugged into this PC, so I read the two consoles directly.

- The ESP32 booted cleanly, WiFi up, I2C slave init OK, both pins pulled high, but the read counter stayed at zero.
- The MCX showed the gateway down on every poll and its bus scan found only the MPU6050, never address 0x42.
- I added a boot-time self-test that counts falling edges on each pin. It saw 10 edges on GPIO21 and 3 on GPIO22. I²C puts nine clock edges per byte on SCL and far fewer on SDA, so the clock is on the pin the sketch treats as SDA.
- With the pin numbers temporarily swapped in code, the link came up immediately: the MCX reported "GW up" with 0 failures at 50 polls a second, and its scan listed the ESP32 gateway.
- I then restored the documented pins and re-flashed, so the board now matches the repo and the docs.

**Why it happened.** On the 30-pin DevKit D21 and D22 are not neighbours. TX0 and RX0 sit between them, so it is easy to land the pair one position off when re-wiring from memory.

**What changed** in esp32_gateway.ino and FIRMWARE.md, uncommitted:

- The boot banner now prints a `verdict :` line. It waits up to 5 s for bus traffic, counts edges, and states in words whether the wires are swapped, one is off the bus, or the bus is silent.
- A new console command `p` holds SDA low for 3 s, then SCL. The MCX diag line must switch to `BUSY` for each. That proves a wire is physically on the MCX bus regardless of pull-ups. The node restarts itself afterwards.
- The firmware guide documents both, and the troubleshooting table has a row for this exact symptom.

**Two things I noticed but did not change.** With the gateway online, the MCX bus scan stopped listing the MPU6050 even though its `sens` output still reads the IMU fine, so the scan's probe is unreliable rather than the sensor. The `sens` line also prints negative IMU values as huge unsigned numbers. Both are MCX-side cosmetics.

That line explains the blank screen: `boot:0x0 ... waiting for download` means GPIO0 was LOW when the chip reset, so it went into flashing mode instead of running the sketch. Nothing is wrong with the firmware. Two things can hold GPIO0 low on this board:

- **The BOOT button** on the DevKit is stuck or being pressed. Check it clicks freely.
- **The Serial Monitor's DTR line** through the board's auto-reset circuit. If you press EN while the monitor holds DTR but not RTS, the board boots into download mode every time.

You're right that nothing in the firmware can damage the chip, and I have no evidence that the wiring or the power did either. Here is what the data rules out and what it leaves.

**Ruled out by evidence**

- Firmware. The same binary ran on this board yesterday, and the last flash verified byte for byte.
- Power. The 3.3 V LED is lit, the USB chip enumerates on every port and cable, and the board was USB-only.
- The I²C wires. The failure persists with both wires removed.
- The MCX. Its bus is healthy and it finds the IMU.

**What I can't determine from the PC** is the physical cause. A mask-ROM bootloader that doesn't answer is below anything software can inspect. The one abnormal clue is the banner you saw before it went silent: `boot:0x0` means every strapping pin on the chip read LOW at once. On a healthy board that value is `0x13`. Several unrelated pins all reading low at the same time points at the chip's IO block or its EN/reset circuit, not at any single pin you touched. The two realistic causes are a static discharge while handling the header, or a latent defect in the module. A board can arrive with a marginal chip, work for a day, and stop. It happens, and it is not something you did.

**One measurement separates "held in reset" from "dead", and the first one is repairable.** With the board on USB, put a multimeter on GND and check:

| Pin | Healthy | If wrong |
|---|---|---|
| EN | 3.3 V, drops to 0 only while EN is pressed | 0 V at rest means the chip is held in reset: a jammed EN button or a failed auto-reset transistor |
| 3V3 | 3.2 to 3.4 V | lower means the rail is loaded by a short in the module |
| IO0 side of the BOOT button | 3.3 V | 0 V at rest means a jammed BOOT button |

If EN sits at 0 V, the module is likely fine. Bridge nothing, but tell me and we'll work out whether the button or the transistor is stuck. If EN is at 3.3 V, 3V3 is correct, and it still prints nothing on EN, the module is gone and there is no repair.
EN reads 3.3V, 3V3 reads 3.3V

That settles it. The chip has power and is not held in reset, its EN and BOOT lines are correct, and it still does not run its own mask ROM. Nothing outside the module can cause that combination. The ESP32 module on this board has failed and it cannot be repaired.

For what it's worth, the most common way a module dies with all rails good is a failed 40 MHz crystal or a cracked solder joint under the metal can. The board flexes when the buttons are pressed hard, and a marginal joint or crystal gives out. That fits a board that worked one day and stopped the next with no electrical abuse. It is not something the wiring, the firmware, or you did.

What you need now:

1. **A replacement ESP32 DevKit.** Any 30-pin or 38-pin board works. Check the regulator by the USB socket before wiring: a fat 4-pin AMS1117 is fine on 9 V, a tiny 5-pin part must be fed 5 V.
2. **Wiring:** SDA to D21, SCL to D22, GND to the star point. On the 30-pin board TX0 and RX0 sit between those two pins.
3. **Sketch:** upload the repo version as it is. The boot banner will confirm `wiring looks right` and the MCX will report `GW up` within seconds.

That is a real finding, and it fits `boot:0x0`. GPIO0 has only three things on it: the BOOT button, the auto-reset transistor driven by the USB chip's DTR/RTS lines, and the chip's own pin. One of those is holding it at ground. Two measurements tell which, and one of the outcomes is not a dead chip.

I'm now holding the port open for 75 seconds with both handshake lines released, which switches the auto-reset transistor off.

1. **Right now, while I hold the port:** measure GPIO0 to GND again. If it rises to 3.3 V, the USB chip's idle DTR/RTS state was pulling it low. That is a board-circuit quirk, not a dead chip, and the fix is a 10 kΩ pull-up from GPIO0 to 3V3.
2. **Then unplug USB** and measure the *resistance* between GPIO0 and GND. Near 0 Ω means the BOOT button is shorted or the chip's pin itself has failed short, which is the classic ESD signature. Tens of kΩ or more means the pin is fine.

Those two numbers are informative:

- **81 kΩ unpowered** means neither the BOOT button nor the pin is shorted. Good.
- **0.5 V when powered** is the interesting one. The chip's own internal pull-up would put GPIO0 near 2 V against 81 kΩ. Something active is pulling it down only while the board has power. There are exactly two candidates.

| Candidate | Why it fits | Fixable? |
|---|---|---|
| The auto-reset transistor, switched on by the USB chip's idle DTR/RTS state | It drives GPIO0 low by design, and the drop across a saturated transistor is a few tenths of a volt | Yes. A 10 kΩ from GPIO0 to 3V3, or fixing the handshake state, and the chip boots normally |
| The chip's GPIO0 pad in latch-up | A latched CMOS pad clamps near 0.5 V only when powered, reads normal unpowered, and a latched chip does not run its ROM | No |

**One test separates them, and I need the board plugged in for it.** Right now no serial device is present. Plug the ESP32 in and tell me. I'll hold the port open with DTR and RTS both released, which switches the transistor off, and you measure GPIO0 to GND during that window. If it climbs to 3.3 V, the transistor is the culprit and the board is repairable. If it stays at 0.5 V with the transistor off, it is the chip.
plugged in, hold the port
Holding COM3 now with DTR and RTS released, for 90 seconds. **Measure GPIO0 to GND now** and tell me the voltage.
still 0.5V

That answers it. With the auto-reset transistor switched off, GPIO0 still sits at 0.5 V, and it reads a clean 81 kΩ with power removed. Only the chip's own GPIO0 pad can do that: it is clamping the pin while powered. That is the signature of a latched-up ESP32, and a latched chip does not run its ROM, which matches everything else we saw. The module is damaged and cannot be repaired.

**Why it happened, without any electrical abuse.** The ESP32 was not fed anything but USB, and that is exactly the problem. The MCX is on its own USB cable and holds SDA and SCL at 3.3 V through the 2 kΩ pull-ups. Any time the ESP32's USB was out while those two wires were still connected to a powered MCX, about 1.6 mA flowed into its GPIO21/22 protection diodes and back-fed the whole chip through its I/O pins. Plugging USB back in with the chip in that state is the textbook trigger for CMOS latch-up. Nothing in the firmware is involved, and no pin was miswired. It just needs the two boards powered at different times while wired together, which is what happens naturally while swapping wires and cables. The first board most likely died the same way, not from 9 V.

**What to do with the replacement:**

- Disconnect the two I²C wires before unplugging either board's USB, and plug USB back in before reconnecting them.
- On the car, power both boards from the same pack so they come up together.
- Optional but cheap insurance: a 470 Ω resistor in series with each I²C wire at the ESP32 end. It limits any injected current below the latch-up threshold and does not affect 400 kHz.

I added this as a warning in FIRMWARE.md under the ESP32 section so it doesn't happen a third time. The sketch is ready as it is. When the new board arrives, plug it in and tell me the port, and I'll flash and verify the whole chain.

The port hold finished cleanly: 90 seconds with both handshake lines released, and the chip sent nothing during the entire window. That confirms the measurement you took was made with the transistor off, so the 0.5 V on GPIO0 comes from the chip itself. The diagnosis stands: latched-up module, replace it.

Nothing else is running now. When the new ESP32 arrives, plug it in and tell me the COM port, and I'll flash the sketch and verify the link with the MCX in one pass.
what is a better board for this project? esp32, esp8266 or a module wifi for arduino?

Stay with an ESP32. The other two are steps down for this specific job, and here is why.

| Option | I²C slave to the MCX | WebSocket server at 10 Hz | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ESP32 DevKit** (what you have) | Hardware I²C slave, works with the existing sketch | Dual core, plenty of headroom | Best fit, zero rework |
| ESP8266 (NodeMCU, Wemos D1) | No hardware I²C slave at all, software-only and unreliable at 400 kHz. The link would have to become UART, and the MCX has no spare UART | Single core, WiFi and the page fight for CPU | Rewrite of both ends, worse result |
| WiFi module for Arduino (ESP-01 with AT firmware, WiFiNINA boards) | An Arduino would sit in the middle, adding a hop and latency | AT-command WebSocket is fragile; NINA works but library support is thin | More parts, more latency, nothing gained |

The design is sound. The gateway needs to be an I²C slave and a self-contained access point, and the classic ESP32 does both with the code already verified. What killed two boards was power sequencing, and that would kill an ESP8266 or a NINA module just the same, since they are all 3.3 V CMOS.

If you are buying anyway, two small upgrades are worth a look:

- **ESP32-S3 DevKitC.** Same Arduino core, same sketch, and its I²C slave supports clock stretching properly, which the classic ESP32 does not. Native USB, so no CH340. You'd only change the two pin numbers.
- **The same classic ESP32 DevKit, 38-pin.** Identical to what you have with the pins spread wider, which makes the D21/D22 mix-up less likely. Cheapest and fastest path to a working demo.

Whichever you pick, fit the two 470 Ω series resistors at the ESP32 end and follow the plug-order rule. That is the actual fix for the failures you have had.

**Schema changes** (uncommitted, in the working tree):

- FULL_SCHEMA.md: §8 now specifies 470 Ω in series with each I²C wire at the ESP32 end, with the latch-up explanation and the plug-order rule. The A.1 and A.6 wiring tables carry the resistor, and §9's parts list has the two extra 470 Ω.
- SCHEMA_WIRING.svg: resistor symbols on both wires at the ESP32 pins in block B, plus a four-line note under the board.
- SCHEMA_SIGNALS.svg: resistor symbols on the two drops from the bus into GPIO21/22, a "Series: 470 Ω" line beside the pull-up note, and note 11 in the numbered list.
- WIRING_4_NODES.svg: resistors drawn on the SCL and SDA wires just before GPIO22/GPIO21, and note 8 in the list.
- esp32_gateway.ino header and FIRMWARE.md say the same thing, so the rule is visible wherever someone starts reading.

**The plug-order rule**

1. Pull the two I²C wires off the ESP32 **before** either board's USB cable comes out.
